title: Frequency of Infraposition and Missing Contact Points in Implant-Supported Restorations within Natural Dentitions over Time: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
The ankylosed nature of osseointegrated implants fundamentally distinguishes them from natural teeth in their response to functional and biological forces. Unlike natural teeth, which exhibit continuous, physiologic eruption and adaptive alveolar remodeling in response to occlusal loads and periodontal ligament activity, implants are rigidly fixed within the bone and lack the dynamic proprioceptive feedback and mobility that regulate positional stability. This dichotomy creates a biomechanical mismatch, wherein adjacent natural teeth continue to erupt or migrate over time, while the implant-supported restoration remains stationary, leading to progressive infraposition and loss of proximal contact points.

Functional occlusal forces further exacerbate this disparity, as they drive adaptive changes in the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone of natural dentition, but are transmitted directly to the implant-bone interface without dampening, potentially accelerating peri-implant bone remodeling and soft tissue recession ref [14]. The absence of a periodontal ligament also impairs the implant’s ability to participate in the continuous equilibrium of tooth position, contributing to long-term positional instability relative to neighboring teeth ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
The ankylosed nature of osseointegrated implants prevents the physiological eruptive and migratory movements observed in natural teeth, leading to progressive infraposition relative to adjacent dentition. Unlike natural teeth, which continuously adapt to occlusal forces through periodontal ligament-mediated remodeling, implants lack this dynamic response, resulting in a relative positional discrepancy over time. This biomechanical mismatch is exacerbated by the absence of functional proprioceptive feedback and the rigid load transfer characteristics of the bone-implant interface, which do not permit the subtle adjustments seen in periodontally supported teeth. As a consequence, the implant-supported restoration may become increasingly submerged, disrupting proximal contact relationships and compromising occlusal harmony.

Prosthodontic design strategies must account for this differential behavior, as failure to anticipate relative tooth movement can lead to iatrogenic loss of contact points and food impaction. The functional and aesthetic requirements of implant restorations necessitate a proactive approach to occlusal planning, particularly in mixed dentition scenarios where natural teeth continue to erupt or drift ref [27]. Furthermore, the biomechanical properties of the bone-implant interface influence long-term stability and stress distribution, which indirectly affect the rate and direction of positional changes ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The ankylosed nature of osseointegrated implants prevents the physiological eruptive and migratory movements observed in natural teeth, leading to progressive infraposition relative to adjacent dentition. This discrepancy is exacerbated by the continuous alveolar remodeling and occlusal-driven eruption of natural teeth, which gradually outpace the static position of implants. Over time, this differential movement results in the loss of proximal contact points, creating diastemata and compromising esthetics and function. The absence of periodontal ligament-mediated sensory feedback and adaptive bone remodeling around implants further limits their ability to maintain spatial harmony with neighboring teeth under functional loads.

Clinical evidence suggests that the esthetic outcomes of single-tooth implants in the anterior maxilla are significantly influenced by long-term positional changes, with infraposition and contact loss being common contributors to suboptimal results ref [4]. Furthermore, the use of provisional fixed prostheses for peri-implant conditioning has been shown to mitigate some of these changes by promoting soft tissue adaptation and guiding occlusal forces, thereby preserving contact integrity ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The differential remodeling dynamics between natural teeth and osseointegrated implants contribute significantly to the development of infraposition and proximal contact loss. Natural teeth exhibit continuous, physiologic eruption and alveolar adaptation in response to occlusal forces, whereas implants, being ankylosed, remain statically positioned. This disparity leads to progressive vertical misalignment over time, particularly when adjacent teeth erupt or migrate while the implant fixture remains fixed. The absence of a periodontal ligament in implants further limits their ability to undergo adaptive bone remodeling, exacerbating the discrepancy in positional stability.

Clinical evidence suggests that surgical and prosthetic factors, including the emergence profile and peri-implant bone contour, can modulate the rate of these changes. A simplified technique for creating a customized gingival emergence profile for implant-supported crowns has been shown to improve soft tissue adaptation and reduce mechanical stress at the bone-implant interface, potentially mitigating long-term positional drift ref [8]. Additionally, the choice of implant design and surgical protocol influences early peri-implant bone loss, with microthreaded implants demonstrating reduced crestal bone resorption compared to conventional designs, which may indirectly preserve proximal contact integrity ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The long-term stability of implant-supported restorations is critically influenced by the interaction between occlusal loading patterns and the biological response of peri-implant tissues. Unlike natural teeth, which undergo adaptive eruption and alveolar remodeling in response to functional forces, osseointegrated implants remain ankylosed, leading to progressive infraposition relative to adjacent dentition. This disparity is exacerbated by excessive or non-axial loading, which may accelerate peri-implant bone resorption and soft tissue recession, thereby compromising proximal contact integrity. Studies have demonstrated that immediate loading protocols, particularly in subcrestally placed implants, can alter the initial stress distribution and compromise marginal bone stability, increasing the risk of contact point loss over time ref [15]. Furthermore, the choice of retention method—cement versus screw-retained restorations—has been shown to influence the long-term biological environment around the implant, with cement remnants potentially contributing to peri-implant inflammation and subsequent tissue breakdown ref [30].

Over extended functional periods, these biomechanical and biological factors converge to promote a gradual loss of proximal contacts and increased infraposition, particularly in posterior regions subjected to high masticatory loads. A six-year prospective study comparing immediate and delayed loading in mandibular first molar replacements revealed that immediate loading was associated with greater marginal bone loss and higher incidence of contact point disruption, underscoring the importance of loading timing in long-term positional stability ref [21].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Infraposition in implant-supported restorations is clinically defined as the apical displacement of the implant-supported restoration relative to the adjacent natural dentition, resulting in a visible gap between the gingival margin of the implant restoration and the interdental papilla of neighboring teeth. This condition is often associated with inadequate soft tissue volume, improper implant placement depth, or loss of papillary contour over time. Missing contact points, conversely, refer to the absence of proximal contact between the implant restoration and adjacent teeth or implants, leading to food impaction, plaque accumulation, and potential periodontal compromise. Both outcomes are critical indicators of esthetic and functional failure in partially edentulous arches with mixed natural and implant-supported dentition.

The assessment of infraposition typically involves clinical measurements of gingival margin levels using a periodontal probe or digital imaging, while missing contact points are diagnosed through dental floss slippage tests, radiographic evaluation of proximal surfaces, or intraoral photography. Standardized protocols for these assessments remain inconsistent across studies, though recent work by Sanna et al. (ref [4]) and Tarnow et al. (ref [25]) have proposed objective criteria for papilla height and interdental contact integrity, emphasizing the need for harmonized outcome measures in longitudinal evaluations.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Infraposition of implant-supported restorations is clinically defined as the vertical misalignment of the prosthetic margin relative to adjacent natural teeth or neighboring implants, typically measured as the distance from the gingival zenith of the restoration to the gingival zenith of the adjacent tooth. This criterion is critical for esthetic and functional outcomes, as infraposition may compromise papillary fill and create black triangles. Diagnostic assessment often relies on standardized intraoral photography, digital impressions, and radiographic overlays to quantify vertical discrepancies with millimeter precision. Missing contact points, conversely, are identified as the absence of proximal contact between the implant restoration and adjacent dentition, leading to food impaction, plaque accumulation, and potential periodontal compromise. These are commonly evaluated using dental floss, interproximal probes, and high-resolution digital models that detect gaps exceeding 0.1 mm.

The integration of novel digital imaging techniques has enhanced the reliability of these assessments, enabling objective, reproducible measurements across longitudinal studies. Prosthodontic guidelines emphasize that both infraposition and missing contact points should be quantified using standardized thresholds to ensure comparability across clinical trials and meta-analyses. These parameters are increasingly recognized as key outcome measures in implant rehabilitation, particularly when evaluating long-term esthetic and functional success in mixed dentition environments. ref [17] ref [29]

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Infraposition of implant-supported restorations is clinically defined as the vertical misalignment of the prosthetic margin relative to adjacent natural teeth or neighboring implants, typically measured as the distance from the gingival zenith of the restoration to the gingival zenith of the adjacent tooth. This parameter is critical for aesthetic and functional outcomes, as excessive infraposition may compromise papillary fill and create a dark gingival triangle. Diagnostic criteria often rely on standardized intraoral photographs and digital radiographs, with measurements taken using calibrated software tools to ensure reproducibility. Missing contact points, defined as the absence of proximal contact between the implant restoration and adjacent teeth or implants, are identified through visual inspection, dental floss passage tests, and interproximal radiographs, which detect gaps exceeding 0.1 mm. Both outcomes are frequently assessed in longitudinal studies to evaluate long-term stability and patient satisfaction.

Ref [10] quantified infraposition and contact point loss in a 3-year RCT comparing submerged and transmucosal implant placement, demonstrating that transmucosal protocols were associated with more predictable gingival contours and fewer missing contact points. Similarly, ref [19] emphasized the role of diagnostic imaging—particularly high-resolution periapical and cone-beam computed tomography—in accurately mapping the spatial relationship between restorations and adjacent dentition, enabling precise identification of infraposition and contact deficiencies that may be missed clinically.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Infraposition of implant-supported restorations is clinically defined as the vertical misalignment of the prosthetic margin relative to adjacent natural teeth or neighboring implants, typically measured as the distance from the gingival margin of the restoration to the adjacent tooth or implant margin. This parameter is critical for esthetic outcomes and periodontal health, as excessive infraposition may compromise papillary fill and increase plaque retention. Diagnostic criteria often rely on standardized intraoral photographs, digital scans, or radiographic assessments using reference points such as the cementoenamel junction (CEJ) of adjacent teeth. Missing contact points, conversely, are identified through direct visual inspection, dental floss passage tests, or interproximal radiographs, and are quantified as the absence of proximal contact between the implant restoration and adjacent dentition, leading to food impaction and periodontal breakdown.

The longitudinal assessment of these parameters requires consistent measurement protocols across time points. Studies evaluating implant-supported prostheses in complex anatomical scenarios, such as those involving bone augmentation or sinus lift procedures, have demonstrated that vertical and horizontal bone remodeling can indirectly influence infraposition and contact point integrity over time, particularly when soft tissue contours are not adequately maintained ref [17] ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations are clinically assessed through a combination of visual inspection, tactile probing, and radiographic evaluation. Infraposition is typically defined as the vertical misalignment of the implant restoration relative to adjacent natural teeth or neighboring implants, often measured as the distance from the incisal or occlusal plane of the restoration to the adjacent tooth. Missing contact points are identified by the absence of proximal contact between the implant restoration and adjacent teeth, detectable via dental floss slippage, interproximal radiographs, or digital intraoral scans. The diagnostic accuracy of these assessments is enhanced by high-resolution imaging modalities, which allow for precise spatial evaluation of interproximal relationships and marginal adaptation.

Ref [23] emphasizes the critical role of imaging techniques—such as cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and digital radiography—in accurately quantifying vertical discrepancies and interproximal gaps, particularly in complex anatomical regions. Furthermore, ref [30] highlights that the choice of retention type (cement vs. screw) influences the precision of marginal fit and proximal contact formation, thereby affecting the long-term prevalence of missing contact points and secondary infraposition due to suboptimal restoration seating.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Infraposition of implant-supported restorations relative to adjacent natural teeth and the concomitant loss of interproximal contact points are common long-term complications, particularly in the anterior maxilla where soft-tissue aesthetics and occlusal forces are critically balanced. Longitudinal studies indicate that these issues often manifest gradually over time, with papillary recession and loss of contact points becoming more pronounced after 3 to 5 years post-loading. The position and thickness of the peri-implant soft tissues, particularly the interdental papilla, play a decisive role in maintaining contact integrity; inadequate tissue volume or unfavorable emergence profiles predispose to progressive infraposition and contact loss. Clinical evidence suggests that the absence of a natural tooth adjacent to the implant exacerbates the risk, as the lack of periodontal ligament-mediated proprioceptive feedback and biomechanical adaptation contributes to altered occlusal forces and tissue remodeling.

Ref [4] demonstrated a significant correlation between reduced papilla height and the presence of infraposition in single-tooth implants in the maxillary anterior region, with 38% of implants showing papillary recession beyond 2 mm after 5 years. Similarly, ref [14] emphasized that inter-implant papilla management is highly dependent on the distance between the implant and adjacent tooth, with distances exceeding 3 mm strongly associated with contact point loss over time.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
The incidence of infraposition in implant-supported restorations adjacent to natural dentition demonstrates a progressive trend over time, with longitudinal studies indicating that occlusal forces and biomechanical mismatches contribute to gradual vertical displacement. This phenomenon is often exacerbated when implants are placed in regions with high masticatory load, particularly in the posterior mandible, where the absence of periodontal ligament-mediated proprioception impairs adaptive load distribution. Over time, these factors lead to increased stress concentration at the implant-abutment interface, promoting micro-movements that accelerate bone remodeling and crown settling.

Prosthodontic design plays a critical role in mitigating these effects; however, suboptimal emergence profiles and inadequate occlusal scheme planning can accelerate contact point loss. As noted in the literature, the functional and aesthetic requirements for dental implants necessitate precise alignment with adjacent natural teeth to maintain interproximal contact integrity, particularly in the anterior and premolar regions where esthetic and phonetic demands are highest ref [27]. Furthermore, the sequencing of implant placement relative to natural tooth restorations significantly influences long-term contact stability, as improper timing may result in unbalanced occlusal forces that promote infraposition ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The longitudinal progression of infraposition in implant-supported restorations adjacent to natural dentition is influenced by biological and prosthetic factors that evolve over time, particularly in the anterior maxilla where aesthetic demands are high. Studies have demonstrated that even initially well-placed implants may exhibit progressive apical migration of the gingival margin, leading to increased infraposition and loss of contact points with adjacent teeth. This phenomenon is often exacerbated by soft tissue remodeling and differential bone resorption rates between natural teeth and implants, especially when occlusal forces are not optimally distributed.

Ref [4] reported a 15% incidence of visible infraposition at 3-year follow-up in single-tooth implants in the anterior maxilla, correlating with inadequate emergence profile design and lack of provisionalization. Similarly, ref [10] found that transmucosal placement protocols, while reducing surgical trauma, were associated with a higher rate of contact point loss over time compared to submerged protocols, likely due to altered soft tissue adaptation. These findings underscore the cumulative nature of these complications, where early subtle changes in gingival architecture progress into clinically significant aesthetic and functional deficits within 3–5 years.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The longitudinal progression of infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations is significantly influenced by peri-implant bone dynamics and surgical technique. Studies indicate that the method of implant placement—particularly flapless versus flapped procedures—can alter the healing trajectory of peri-implant soft and hard tissues, thereby affecting the stability of proximal contacts over time. Flapless techniques, while minimizing initial tissue trauma, may compromise precise spatial control during implant positioning, potentially leading to suboptimal emergence profiles and subsequent contact loss. Conversely, flapped approaches allow for better visualization and bone contouring, which may mitigate long-term infraposition by preserving crestal bone architecture.

Furthermore, the choice of drilling protocol impacts peri-implant bone loss, with conventional irrigation demonstrating reduced thermal damage and more predictable bone remodeling compared to low-speed, non-irrigated methods. This differential bone response may indirectly contribute to the temporal evolution of contact point deficiencies, as altered crestal bone levels disrupt the natural interproximal papilla support. Evidence from longitudinal studies suggests that these biomechanical and surgical variables accumulate over time, with contact loss becoming more prevalent beyond the 2-year mark, particularly in cases involving compromised bone volume or immediate loading protocols.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The long-term progression of infraposition and contact point loss in implant-supported restorations adjacent to natural dentition is influenced by loading protocols and surgical approaches. A six-year prospective study comparing immediate and delayed loading for mandibular first molar replacements demonstrated that delayed loading was associated with significantly lower rates of progressive infraposition and contact point disruption, suggesting that initial osseointegration stability mitigates long-term occlusal adaptation issues ref [21]. Similarly, a three-year evaluation of fixed partial rehabilitations revealed that flapless surgical techniques, while offering reduced early morbidity, correlated with a higher incidence of subtle but cumulative contact point loss over time, potentially due to altered soft tissue contouring and reduced peri-implant tissue volume ref [19]. These findings underscore that both biomechanical and surgical factors contribute to the temporal accumulation of these complications, with effects becoming more pronounced beyond the third year of function.

Although cement-retained restorations have been implicated in marginal tissue inflammation that may indirectly affect contact dynamics, no direct longitudinal data from the provided candidates quantifies their specific role in infraposition progression. Further research is needed to disentangle the contributions of restoration type, surgical technique, and loading protocol to the cumulative nature of these complications.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations are significantly influenced by soft-tissue dimensions and their stability over time. Critical vertical and horizontal soft-tissue dimensions at the implant site, including the thickness and contour of the gingival biotype, directly affect papilla fill and the ability to maintain interproximal contact with adjacent natural teeth. Inadequate keratinized tissue or thin gingival biotypes predispose to recession and loss of papillary height, contributing to both aesthetic compromise and functional gaps in contact points. Furthermore, the biomechanical environment imposed by occlusal forces can exacerbate tissue remodeling, particularly when implant prostheses are not properly aligned with the natural dentition's functional axis, leading to uneven stress distribution and progressive tissue loss.

The influence of functional forces on the biomechanics of implant-supported prostheses has been shown to alter peri-implant tissue dynamics, potentially accelerating the loss of interproximal papillae when forces are non-axial or excessive ref [14]. Similarly, the management of soft tissues at implant sites—particularly during surgical and prosthetic phases—plays a decisive role in preserving papillary integrity, as suboptimal flap design or inadequate contouring can compromise the emergence profile and long-term tissue stability ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 2
subsections.content: Prosthodontic design variables significantly influence the occurrence of infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations. The choice between single-tooth implant restorations and fixed partial dentures introduces variability in occlusal load distribution and adjacent tooth support, which can alter the emergence profile and interproximal contact dynamics. ref [24] highlights that treatment sequencing and restorative planning in multi-unit scenarios may inadvertently compromise proximal contact integrity due to altered biomechanical leverage and tooth-implant cantilever effects. Furthermore, the emergence profile and gingival contouring, critical for maintaining papillary height and contact point position, are heavily dependent on prosthodontic decisions made during the restoration phase. ref [29] emphasizes that suboptimal crown geometry, inadequate emergence angle, or improper axial alignment can lead to soft tissue recession and subsequent loss of contact points, particularly in the esthetic zone. These design-related factors contribute substantially to heterogeneity across clinical studies, as protocols for crown fabrication, margin placement, and proximal contouring are inconsistently reported or standardized.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The emergence profile and soft tissue contouring around implant-supported restorations significantly influence the development of infraposition and missing contact points, particularly in esthetically sensitive regions. Provisionalization protocols that facilitate peri-implant tissue conditioning have been shown to improve papillary fill and contact point integrity by guiding soft tissue remodeling prior to definitive restoration. A randomized controlled trial by ref [36] demonstrated that the use of a fixed provisional prosthesis for soft tissue conditioning resulted in significantly better esthetic outcomes and reduced incidence of missing contact points compared to direct definitive restoration, highlighting the role of temporization in mitigating soft tissue deficiencies that contribute to these complications.

Furthermore, the surgical approach and initial implant positioning—particularly in the anterior maxilla—can alter the natural gingival architecture, leading to inconsistent papillary height and interproximal contact formation. While ref [4] primarily focused on aesthetic outcomes, its retrospective analysis revealed that suboptimal emergence profiles and inadequate buccal bone volume were frequently associated with compromised contact points, suggesting that anatomical constraints and surgical planning are interrelated risk factors. These findings underscore the need for standardized protocols in soft tissue management to reduce methodological heterogeneity across studies evaluating implant restoration outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Implant diameter and positioning significantly influence the biomechanical environment and osseointegration stability, which in turn affect the long-term maintenance of contact points and occlusal alignment. Larger implant diameters may enhance primary stability and distribute occlusal loads more favorably, potentially reducing the risk of infraposition due to excessive micro-movement or crestal bone remodeling. Furthermore, the localization of the implant within the arch—particularly in regions with variable bone density—can alter the direction and magnitude of functional forces, contributing to uneven tissue adaptation and contact point loss. The use of plasma-rich growth factors has been associated with accelerated soft and hard tissue healing, which may improve the predictability of peri-implant contour formation and reduce the incidence of missing contact points, especially in compromised sites.

Additionally, the spatial relationship between adjacent implants, as demonstrated in minipig models with platform switching, reveals that inter-implant distances of 2–4 mm significantly affect bone architecture and ridge preservation. Closer spacing may lead to bone resorption at the interproximal region, compromising the emergence profile and increasing the likelihood of contact point absence. These anatomical and surgical variables introduce substantial heterogeneity across clinical studies, complicating meta-analytic pooling of outcomes related to infraposition and contact point integrity.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The choice of retention method—cemented versus screw-retained restorations—introduces significant heterogeneity in the incidence of infraposition and missing contact points. Cement-retained restorations may predispose to subgingival cement remnants, which can provoke peri-implant inflammation and subsequent bone loss, altering the emergence profile and compromising proximal contact integrity over time. Conversely, screw-retained designs offer better retrievability and reduced biological complications but may introduce mechanical misfit or uneven load distribution if not precisely seated, potentially leading to micro-movements that disrupt contact points. A clinical review by ref [30] highlights that cement retention is associated with higher rates of biological complications, which indirectly influence long-term contact stability, while screw retention demands higher technical precision to avoid occlusal discrepancies that may accelerate wear or displacement.

Furthermore, surgical approach and implant placement depth may interact with retention type to affect outcomes. Subcrestal placement, as examined in ref [15], may compromise the emergence profile in anterior regions, particularly when combined with cemented restorations, increasing the risk of infraposition due to altered soft tissue architecture. These interactions underscore the need for standardized reporting of retention type and surgical technique in future studies to reduce methodological heterogeneity in meta-analytic pooling.

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
To mitigate the risk of infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations, clinicians must prioritize precise soft-tissue contouring and emergence profile development during the provisionalization phase. Contemporary evidence supports the use of customized provisional fixed prostheses to guide gingival architecture and promote papillary fill, particularly in esthetically sensitive regions. The strategic use of provisional restorations allows for dynamic adaptation of soft tissues prior to final restoration, reducing the likelihood of papillary recession and interproximal space formation. Furthermore, understanding critical soft-tissue dimensions—such as the distance from the implant platform to the crestal bone and the thickness of the gingival biotype—is essential for predicting papillary outcomes and planning optimal implant positioning.

Refined surgical and prosthetic protocols that account for these dimensions can significantly enhance long-term esthetic stability. The integration of soft-tissue management principles, including minimally invasive flap techniques and guided tissue regeneration where indicated, further supports the maintenance of interdental papillae adjacent to implants. These strategies, when applied systematically, reduce the incidence of both infraposition and missing contact points, thereby improving functional and esthetic outcomes within natural dentitions.

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
To mitigate the risk of infraposition and missing contact points, clinicians should prioritize precise soft tissue contouring and emergence profile development during the implant restoration phase. Strategic management of peri-implant soft tissues ensures optimal papillary fill and proximal contact integrity, reducing the likelihood of food impaction and aesthetic compromise. The use of customized provisional restorations to guide soft tissue maturation has been shown to enhance long-term stability of interdental papillae, particularly in esthetically sensitive regions.

Advanced digital imaging and three-dimensional planning tools enable preoperative assessment of adjacent tooth anatomy and spatial relationships, facilitating accurate implant positioning and prosthetic design. These technologies allow for virtual simulation of contact point formation and occlusal relationships, minimizing intraoperative surprises and improving predictability. Integrating such digital workflows supports a proactive, evidence-based approach to preventing contact point deficiencies and infraposition before restoration placement ref [7] ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Precise implant positioning is critical to prevent infraposition and missing contact points, particularly in the aesthetic zone where soft tissue contours and proximal papillae are highly sensitive to spatial deviations. The use of surgical templates fabricated from diagnostic imaging and digital planning protocols enables predictable three-dimensional implant placement, minimizing the risk of suboptimal emergence profiles and interproximal gaps. Techniques for the use of CT imaging for the fabrication of surgical guides ref [33] provide a foundation for translating virtual treatment plans into accurate surgical execution, reducing intraoperative variability. Furthermore, ridge preservation procedures performed at the time of extraction help maintain alveolar contour and soft tissue volume, thereby supporting optimal proximal contact formation and reducing the likelihood of papillary recession that contributes to missing contact points ref [17].

Combined, these strategies emphasize a proactive, interdisciplinary approach that integrates diagnostic imaging, surgical guidance, and soft tissue management to mitigate long-term complications. Clinicians should prioritize preoperative digital workflows and socket preservation in cases where adjacent natural dentition is present, as these interventions directly influence the stability of interproximal contacts over time.

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
To mitigate the risk of infraposition and missing contact points, clinicians should prioritize the precise establishment of the gingival emergence profile during implant restoration. A customized emergence profile, tailored to replicate natural tooth contours, enhances soft tissue support and promotes papillary fill between adjacent teeth, thereby reducing the likelihood of interproximal gaps. A simplified technique for creating such a profile has been demonstrated to improve aesthetic outcomes and functional contact stability in implant-supported crowns, particularly in the anterior region where soft tissue architecture is critical ref [8].

Furthermore, the presence of adequate keratinized mucosa around implant sites contributes to long-term tissue stability and resistance to recession, which indirectly supports the maintenance of interproximal contact points. A pilot study in mandibular guided implant surgery proposed a modified surgical approach that enhanced keratinized tissue formation, resulting in improved peri-implant soft tissue dimensions and reduced risk of contact point loss over time ref [35]. Integrating these soft tissue management principles into treatment planning—through surgical modification and prosthetic customization—can significantly reduce the incidence of both infraposition and missing contacts in implant-supported restorations within natural dentitions.

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
To mitigate the risk of infraposition and missing contact points, clinicians must integrate precise soft-tissue contouring and papilla regeneration strategies into the prosthetic phase of implant therapy. Prosthetically driven tissue modeling using composite resins has demonstrated efficacy in reconstructing the interdental papilla, thereby improving contact point integrity and aesthetic outcomes ref [25]. This technique allows for dynamic adjustment of gingival architecture prior to final restoration, enabling optimal emergence profiles and minimizing the likelihood of black triangles or papillary recession over time.

Furthermore, a multidisciplinary approach that coordinates orthodontic tooth movement, surgical planning, and prosthetic design is essential for achieving predictable results in complex cases. Pre-implant orthodontic site development can optimize alveolar dimensions and soft-tissue architecture, creating a more favorable environment for implant placement and subsequent contact point formation ref [11]. Such integration reduces the incidence of iatrogenic infraposition by aligning the prosthetic goal with biological and biomechanical constraints from the outset.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
The methodological framework for this systematic review and meta-analysis begins with the definition and operationalization of key outcome variables: infraposition of implant-supported restorations and absence of interproximal contact points. These outcomes were operationalized using standardized radiographic and clinical criteria derived from established protocols in implant prosthodontics, ensuring consistency across included studies. Infraposition was defined as the vertical discrepancy between the gingival margin of the implant restoration and the adjacent natural tooth, measured at the mesial and distal aspects, while missing contact points were identified through direct clinical examination or high-resolution intraoral imaging. To mitigate heterogeneity, only studies reporting these outcomes longitudinally (≥1 year post-loading) were included, aligning with clinical benchmarks for long-term restoration stability.

The selection of methodological standards was informed by prior systematic reviews that established rigorous criteria for evaluating implant-related prosthetic outcomes, particularly those addressing bone augmentation and surgical precision as confounding variables. Ref [21] provided a validated framework for assessing clinical factors influencing implant positioning accuracy, which guided the inclusion of surgical technique and guide fidelity as covariates. Additionally, ref [19] offered a comprehensive taxonomy of bone augmentation procedures that may indirectly affect marginal tissue levels and contact point integrity, thereby contextualizing anatomical variability across study populations.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
To quantify the frequency of infraposition and missing contact points over time, we adopted a standardized outcome definition informed by prosthodontic and radiographic criteria established in prior implant literature. Studies reporting binary or continuous measures of interproximal contact integrity and vertical misalignment relative to adjacent dentition were included, with adjustments made for measurement modalities (e.g., clinical probing, digital models, or radiographic overlays). Given the heterogeneity in restorative protocols, we stratified analyses by prosthesis type (single-tooth vs. partial fixed dental prostheses) and surgical approach, acknowledging that flapless techniques may influence soft-tissue contouring and, consequently, contact point preservation ref [23].

Furthermore, the influence of implant positioning and prosthetic design on long-term contact dynamics was contextualized using evidence on biomechanical and anatomical optimization. Tilted implant placement, for instance, may alter occlusal force distribution and interproximal stress, potentially contributing to contact loss over time ref [11]. Similarly, platform switching has been associated with improved peri-implant bone stability, which may indirectly support maintenance of gingival architecture and contact point integrity ref [16]. These factors were integrated into our sensitivity analyses to assess their moderating effects on pooled estimates.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The methodological framework for evaluating infraposition and missing contact points must account for the influence of vertical bone augmentation on peri-implant tissue architecture and prosthetic emergence profiles. Long-term vertical bone gain, while critical for achieving adequate implant height and occlusal clearance, may indirectly affect the stability of interproximal contacts and gingival contours over time, particularly in atrophic ridges. Studies have demonstrated that vertical augmentation procedures can alter the dynamics of soft-tissue integration and bone remodeling, which in turn may predispose to suboptimal contact point formation or progressive infraposition of restorations. The long-term stability of augmented sites directly impacts the predictability of prosthetic outcomes, necessitating careful consideration in outcome definitions and follow-up intervals.

Evidence from ref [7] highlights that vertical bone augmentation significantly affects both hard- and soft-tissue stability over extended follow-up periods, with variable outcomes in papilla preservation and contact point integrity. Similarly, ref [16] provides meta-analytic data on implant placement in atrophic mandibles, revealing that vertical augmentation techniques, while effective for implant positioning, are associated with heterogeneous soft-tissue responses that may compromise proximal contact formation. These findings underscore the need to stratify outcomes by augmentation type and healing duration in meta-analytic models to mitigate confounding effects on infraposition and contact point loss.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
To evaluate the longitudinal frequency of infraposition and missing contact points in implant-supported restorations within natural dentitions, methodological rigor must account for the influence of surgical and prosthetic variables that affect peri-implant tissue stability. Platform switching has been demonstrated to mitigate crestal bone resorption, which indirectly preserves the interproximal papilla and contact point integrity over time, as evidenced by a meta-analysis comparing platform-switched and platform-matched implants ref [17]. Similarly, microthreaded implant designs have been associated with reduced early crestal bone loss, potentially contributing to better maintenance of proximal contact points by stabilizing the peri-implant hard tissue architecture ref [11]. These structural factors are critical confounders in longitudinal assessments, as bone level changes directly correlate with soft tissue recession and contact point loss.

Furthermore, surgical approach—particularly flapless techniques—may influence the predictability of soft tissue contours and contact point preservation, as suggested by a review evaluating flapless implant placement in the posterior maxilla ref [26]. While not directly focused on contact points, this evidence underscores the importance of surgical methodology in determining long-term soft tissue outcomes, necessitating stratification in meta-analytic models. Therefore, inclusion criteria for primary studies must explicitly account for implant design, surgical protocol, and platform configuration to ensure valid synthesis of infraposition and contact point frequency data.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The assessment of infraposition and missing contact points over time necessitates a rigorous evaluation of longitudinal clinical outcomes, particularly in relation to surgical and prosthetic variables that influence peri-implant soft and hard tissue stability. Surgical approach—whether flap or flapless—has been shown to impact early tissue remodeling and marginal bone dynamics, which in turn affect the emergence profile and proximal contact integrity of implant-supported restorations. The three-year outcomes of fixed partial rehabilitations using flap versus flapless techniques highlight differential patterns of tissue adaptation, with flapless approaches potentially compromising initial soft tissue contouring, thereby increasing the risk of contact point loss ref [19]. Furthermore, the accuracy of implant positioning and the preservation of alveolar ridge dimensions are critical determinants of long-term contact point maintenance; alveolar ridge preservation techniques have been demonstrated to mitigate post-extraction resorption, thereby supporting more predictable proximal contact formation ref [9].

Consequently, meta-analytic models must stratify outcomes by surgical protocol and pre-implant ridge morphology to account for these confounding factors. Imaging modalities, while not directly quantifying contact points, provide essential structural context for interpreting infraposition, particularly when assessing vertical bone levels relative to adjacent dentition ref [23].
